section: Articles 20, 21, 21A and 22 - protection in conviction, life and liberty, education, preventive detention
subsections: Article 21 derived rights recognised by courts

Right to die and euthanasia cases

accepted.s: Which one of the following cases recognised the right to travel abroad as a facet of Article 21?
o: Subhash Kumar v. State of Bihar
Olga Tellis v. Bombay Municipal Corporation
Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India
Hussainara Khatoon v. State of Bihar
accepted.x: Maneka Gandhi (1978) recognised the right to travel abroad under Article 21. Satwant Singh Sawhney (1967) had earlier dealt with the same right.
accepted.tq: Direct case-to-right recall using closely related Article 21 cases as distractors.
accepted.sec: Article 21 derived rights recognised by courts  [APPSC]

accepted.s: The right to marry a person of one’s choice was recognised in which of the following cases?
o: Common Cause v. Union of India
Supriyo Chakraborty v. Union of India
Mohini Jain v. State of Karnataka
accepted.x: Shafin Jahan, popularly associated with the Hadiya case, recognised the individual’s choice of partner under Article 21 in 2018.
accepted.tq: Confusable-case discrimination between marriage, privacy and euthanasia decisions.
accepted.sec: Article 21 derived rights recognised by courts  [APPSC]

accepted.s: With reference to rights read into Article 21, which of the following pairs is correctly matched?
o: Free legal aid — Subhash Kumar case
Emergency medical care — Maneka Gandhi case
accepted.x: Olga Tellis v. Bombay Municipal Corporation (1985) recognised livelihood as a component of the right to life. The other cases are associated with speedy trial, clean environment and travel abroad respectively.
accepted.tq: Start from the sure case-right pair and eliminate swapped authorities.
accepted.sec: Article 21 derived rights recognised by courts  [APPSC]

accepted.s:
Consider the following statements regarding rights recognised under Article 21:
1. Hussainara Khatoon recognised speedy trial as a component of Article 21.
2. Subhash Kumar recognised the right to a clean environment.
3. Chameli Singh recognised the right to shelter.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
accepted.x: All three statements are correct. Hussainara Khatoon dealt with speedy trial, Subhash Kumar with a clean environment, and Chameli Singh with shelter.
accepted.tq: Statement-combination question requiring separate case-right identification.
accepted.sec: Article 21 derived rights recognised by courts  [APPSC]

accepted.s: The right to emergency medical care under Article 21 was recognised in which case?
o: M.H. Hoskot v. State of Maharashtra
K.A. Najeeb v. Union of India
Paschim Banga Khet Mazdoor Samity v. State of West Bengal
accepted.x: Paschim Banga Khet Mazdoor Samity (1996) recognised the obligation to provide emergency medical care as part of Article 21.
accepted.tq: Direct case recall with distractors drawn from other Article 21 rights.
accepted.sec: Article 21 derived rights recognised by courts  [APPSC]

accepted.s: M.H. Hoskot v. State of Maharashtra is associated with which of the following rights under Article 21?
o: Right to marry a person of choice
accepted.x: M.H. Hoskot (1978) is associated with free legal aid as a component of fair procedure and personal liberty.
accepted.tq: One-fact case association using nearby Article 21 doctrines as distractors.
accepted.sec: Article 21 derived rights recognised by courts  [APPSC]

accepted.s: Which of the following pairs is NOT correctly matched?
o: Common Cause — Right to marry as an unqualified fundamental right
K.A. Najeeb — Reaffirmation of speedy trial
accepted.x: Common Cause (2018) recognised the right to die with dignity and the validity of living wills. Supriyo Chakraborty (2023) held that there is no unqualified fundamental right to marry as such.
accepted.tq: Find the wrong case-holding pair, especially the swapped marriage and euthanasia doctrines.
accepted.sec: Article 21 derived rights recognised by courts  [APPSC]

accepted.s: In which case did the Supreme Court recognise the right to privacy as a fundamental right under Article 21?
o: Justice K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India
Olga Tellis v. Bombay Municipal Corporation
accepted.x: Justice K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India (2017) recognised privacy as a fundamental right under Article 21.
accepted.tq: Direct identification of the landmark privacy case.
accepted.sec: Article 21 derived rights recognised by courts  [APPSC]

accepted.s: Which one of the following statements correctly describes the effect of the Supriyo Chakraborty judgment of 2023?
o: It recognised an unqualified fundamental right to marry for all persons.
It declared the right to privacy unconstitutional.
It held that travel abroad is not protected under Article 21.
It held that there is no fundamental right to marry as such, while other Article 21 rights remain recognised.
accepted.x: Supriyo Chakraborty held that there is no unqualified fundamental right to marry as such. This does not remove Article 21 protection for dignity, privacy or choice of partner.
accepted.tq: Discriminate between the right to choose a partner and an unqualified right to marry.
accepted.sec: Article 21 derived rights recognised by courts  [APPSC]

accepted.s:
Consider the following statements about Article 21:
1. It is available to both citizens and non-citizens.
2. It has been interpreted to include dignity, health and mental health.
3. It includes protection against solitary confinement and compensation for violation of rights.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
accepted.x: Article 21 protects citizens and non-citizens and has been expansively interpreted to include dignity, health, mental health, protection against solitary confinement and compensation for violations.
accepted.tq: Cumulative statement testing of the expanding scope of a constitutional right.
accepted.sec: Article 21 derived rights recognised by courts  [APPSC]

accepted.s: Which case recognised the right to walk safely on footpaths by invoking Articles 19(1)(d) and 21 and referred to restitutionary remedies?
o: Chameli Singh v. State of Uttar Pradesh
M.H. Hoskot v. State of Maharashtra
Paschim Banga Khet Mazdoor Samity v. State of West Bengal
accepted.x: Maniyar Iliyaz v. P. Ayyappan (2026) connected safe walking on footpaths with Articles 19(1)(d) and 21 and referred to restitutionary remedies.
accepted.tq: Current judicial-development recall with precise constitutional provisions.
accepted.sec: Article 21 derived rights recognised by courts  [APPSC]

accepted.s: Article 20(1) primarily protects a person against which of the following?
o: Ex post facto criminal law imposing conviction or a heavier penalty
Retrospective application of every civil law
accepted.x: Article 20(1) prohibits conviction under a criminal law that was not in force when the act was committed and prohibits a heavier penalty than the one applicable at that time.
accepted.tq: Direct clause-to-protection recall, distinguishing criminal from civil consequences.
accepted.sec: Article 20 - ex post facto law, double jeopardy, self-incrimination, what it does not contain  [APPSC]

accepted.s:
Consider the following statements regarding Article 20(1):
1. It applies to criminal laws.
2. It prohibits a heavier penalty than the penalty applicable when the offence was committed.
3. It bars the conduct of a trial itself in every case involving a later-enacted criminal law.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
accepted.x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct. Article 20(1) bars conviction and a greater penalty, but it does not necessarily bar the trial itself.
accepted.tq: Test the precise scope of a protection rather than its broad slogan.
accepted.sec: Article 20 - ex post facto law, double jeopardy, self-incrimination, what it does not contain  [APPSC]

accepted.s: The protection against double jeopardy under Article 20(2) means that a person shall not be:
o: Prosecuted and punished more than once for the same offence
Subjected to both civil and criminal proceedings
Arrested and questioned twice for any purpose
accepted.x: Article 20(2) protects against being prosecuted and punished twice for the same offence. Its constitutional scope concerns prosecution and punishment by a court or judicial tribunal.
accepted.tq: Exact-word discrimination between prosecution, punishment and other proceedings.
accepted.sec: Article 20 - ex post facto law, double jeopardy, self-incrimination, what it does not contain  [APPSC]

accepted.s: Which of the following is outside the constitutional protection against double jeopardy under Article 20(2), as stated in the recognised scope of the provision?
o: A second judicial punishment for the same offence
Prosecution and punishment by a court
accepted.x: Article 20(2) covers prosecution and punishment by a court or judicial tribunal, but it does not extend to departmental proceedings.
accepted.tq: Identify the exception by distinguishing judicial punishment from departmental action.
accepted.sec: Article 20 - ex post facto law, double jeopardy, self-incrimination, what it does not contain  [APPSC]

accepted.s:
With reference to Article 20(3), consider the following statements:
1. It applies to criminal proceedings.
2. It covers oral and documentary testimony.
3. It generally treats fingerprints and physical specimens as testimonial self-incrimination.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
accepted.x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct. Physical evidence such as fingerprints is not treated as testimonial compulsion under Article 20(3), as recognised in Kathi Kalu Oghad (1961).
accepted.tq: Separate testimonial evidence from physical evidence before selecting the combination.
accepted.sec: Article 20 - ex post facto law, double jeopardy, self-incrimination, what it does not contain  [APPSC]

accepted.s: Which of the following forms of evidence was held not to be covered by the protection against self-incrimination in Kathi Kalu Oghad (1961)?
o: A compelled written statement describing the offence
accepted.x: Kathi Kalu Oghad (1961) distinguished physical evidence such as fingerprints from testimonial compulsion protected by Article 20(3).
accepted.tq: Confusable-pair discrimination between physical evidence and testimony.
accepted.sec: Article 20 - ex post facto law, double jeopardy, self-incrimination, what it does not contain  [APPSC]

accepted.s: In Selvi v. State of Karnataka (2010), the Supreme Court held that which of the following, when conducted without consent, violates Article 20(3)?
o: Verification of age through official records
accepted.x: Selvi (2010) held that narco-analysis, polygraph examination and brain-mapping without consent violate the protection against testimonial compulsion under Article 20(3).
accepted.tq: Direct case-to-doctrine recall using physical-evidence distractors.
accepted.sec: Article 20 - ex post facto law, double jeopardy, self-incrimination, what it does not contain  [APPSC]

accepted.s: Which of the following correctly describes the applicability of Article 20?
o: It is available only during an Emergency.
It is available only to Indian citizens.
It is available to citizens, foreigners and legal persons such as companies.
It is available only to natural persons present in India.
accepted.x: The protections under Article 20 are available to citizens, foreigners and legal persons such as companies, subject to the nature of the particular protection.
accepted.tq: Membership and coverage trap involving citizens, aliens and companies.
accepted.sec: Article 20 - ex post facto law, double jeopardy, self-incrimination, what it does not contain  [APPSC]

accepted.s: Which one of the following is NOT covered by Article 20 protections?
o: Double prosecution and punishment for the same offence
accepted.x: Article 20 does not cover retrospective civil or tax laws. Article 20(1) is confined to ex post facto criminal laws.
accepted.tq: Find the excluded category by separating criminal law from civil and tax law.
accepted.sec: Article 20 - ex post facto law, double jeopardy, self-incrimination, what it does not contain  [APPSC]

accepted.s: Under the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, the provision corresponding to the protection against double jeopardy is contained in:
accepted.x: Section 337 of the BNSS contains the provision relating to double jeopardy; it corresponds to the earlier Section 300 of the CrPC.
accepted.tq: Section-number discrimination between the new code and the repealed CrPC provision.
accepted.sec: Article 20 - ex post facto law, double jeopardy, self-incrimination, what it does not contain  [APPSC]

accepted.s: The protections under Article 20 are regarded as non-suspendable during an Emergency. Which of the following best reflects this position?
o: Article 20 protections may be suspended by executive order alone.
Article 20 applies only after the Emergency is withdrawn.
Article 20 protects only citizens during an Emergency.
Article 20 protections continue even during an Emergency.
accepted.x: The protections guaranteed by Article 20 are non-suspendable during an Emergency. They are not confined to citizens alone.
accepted.tq: Apply the constitutional protection to an Emergency situation without confusing it with ordinary restrictions.
accepted.sec: Article 20 - ex post facto law, double jeopardy, self-incrimination, what it does not contain  [APPSC]

accepted.s:
Arrange the following cases in chronological order:
A. Common Cause
B. P. Rathinam
C. Gian Kaur
D. Aruna Shanbaug
accepted.x: P. Rathinam was decided in 1994, Gian Kaur in 1996, Aruna Shanbaug in 2011 and Common Cause in 2018.
accepted.tq: Use the earliest and latest cases first, then place the two intervening rulings.
accepted.sec: Right to die and euthanasia cases  [APPSC]

accepted.s: What was the ruling in P. Rathinam (1994)?
o: A fundamental right to marry was recognised.
Passive euthanasia was permitted under High Court supervision.
Section 309 IPC was upheld without qualification.
Section 309 IPC, dealing with attempted suicide, was held unconstitutional.
accepted.x: P. Rathinam (1994) held Section 309 IPC unconstitutional and treated suicide as something that should not be criminally punished.
accepted.tq: Direct case-holding recall with nearby euthanasia rulings as distractors.
accepted.sec: Right to die and euthanasia cases  [APPSC]

accepted.s: Which case overruled the decision in P. Rathinam and held that there is no right to die, while recognising a right to die with dignity?
accepted.x: Gian Kaur v. State of Punjab (1996) overruled P. Rathinam. It held that there is no right to death but recognised the right to die with dignity and upheld Section 309 IPC.
accepted.tq: Identify the overruling case by separating right to die from right to die with dignity.
accepted.sec: Right to die and euthanasia cases  [APPSC]

accepted.s:
Consider the following statements about the right to die and euthanasia cases:
1. Maruti Shripati Dubal held that the right to die formed part of Article 21.
2. Gian Kaur overruled the position in Maruti Shripati Dubal and P. Rathinam.
3. Common Cause recognised the right to die with dignity as a fundamental right under Article 21.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
accepted.x: Statements 1 and 3 are correct. Gian Kaur overruled P. Rathinam, but the material does not state that it overruled Maruti Shripati Dubal in the same formulation; the Bombay High Court decision preceded Rathinam.
accepted.tq: Avoid overextending an overruling judgment beyond the specific case identified.
accepted.sec: Right to die and euthanasia cases  [APPSC]

accepted.s: Which of the following correctly describes the decision in Aruna Shanbaug (2011)?
o: The euthanasia plea was rejected, but passive euthanasia was allowed under strict conditions and High Court supervision.
A living will was declared invalid in every circumstance.
Active euthanasia was made a general fundamental right.
accepted.x: In Aruna Shanbaug (2011), the plea was rejected, but passive euthanasia was permitted under strict conditions and High Court supervision.
accepted.tq: Distinguish passive euthanasia from active euthanasia and from the later living-will ruling.
accepted.sec: Right to die and euthanasia cases  [APPSC]

accepted.s: The validity of a living will or advance directive in the context of the right to die with dignity was recognised in:
accepted.x: Common Cause (2018) recognised the right to die with dignity as part of Article 21 and upheld the validity of a living will or advance directive.
accepted.tq: Direct identification of the latest landmark holding in a sequence of related cases.
accepted.sec: Right to die and euthanasia cases  [APPSC]

accepted.s: With regard to attempted suicide in India, which of the following statements is correct?
o: The Mental Healthcare Act, 2017 created a general offence of attempted suicide.
The BNS decriminalised every act intended to compel a public servant.
The Mental Healthcare Act, 2017 decriminalised attempted suicide in effect, and the BNS has no general offence of attempted suicide.
The BNS retained Section 309 IPC unchanged as a general offence.
accepted.x: The Mental Healthcare Act, 2017 decriminalised attempted suicide in effect. The BNS, in force from 1 July 2024, contains no general offence of attempted suicide.
accepted.tq: Compare the position under the Mental Healthcare Act and the post-IPC BNS framework.
accepted.sec: Right to die and euthanasia cases  [APPSC]

accepted.s: Under Section 226 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, an attempt to commit suicide is punishable when it is made for the purpose of:
o: Compelling or restraining a public servant from discharging official duties
accepted.x: Section 226 BNS applies only to an attempt to compel or restrain a public servant from exercising lawful powers or discharging official duties; it is not a general offence of attempted suicide.
accepted.tq: Apply the narrow statutory exception instead of treating it as a general prohibition.
accepted.sec: Right to die and euthanasia cases  [APPSC]

accepted.s: The Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 replaced the Indian Penal Code with effect from:
accepted.x: The Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 came into force on 1 July 2024. It does not retain a general offence of attempted suicide corresponding to Section 309 IPC.
accepted.tq: Date-based recall of the transition from IPC to BNS.
accepted.sec: Right to die and euthanasia cases  [APPSC]
